opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think I came to it sideways. My background was really in linguistics; I was the kind of kid who got obsessed with grammars of languages I'd never speak, trying to figure out the hidden rules that make a sentence feel right or wrong. So when language models suddenly got good, my first reaction wasn't "wow, what can we build with this?" It was "wait, how is it doing that?" These systems clearly picked up something about syntax and meaning, and nobody had written those rules down for them. That felt like the most interesting puzzle in the world.

Interpretability is basically the science of answering that question. It treats the model like a natural object you can study: form hypotheses about what's going on inside, then intervene and test them. That last part is what really hooked me. With humans, linguists and cognitive scientists can only poke at the brain indirectly. With a neural network, you have every single activation. You can swap one internal representation for another and see exactly how the behavior changes. It's a kind of experimental access that scientists in most fields would kill for.

There's also a practical side I care about. These models are being deployed everywhere, and "it works on the benchmark" isn't a satisfying level of understanding for something that consequential. If we want to trust them, fix them when they break, or steer them, we need real causal explanations of their internal mechanisms, not just correlations.

So it's a mix of things: scientific curiosity carried over from linguistics, the unusually clean experimental setup, and a sense that this understanding is going to matter a lot. Interpretability sits right where all three meet, so it felt less like choosing a direction and more like realizing I'd already been heading there.

r001.rationale: He says his first response to capable language models was to ask how they worked, especially how they learned syntax and meaning, and calls that the puzzle that drew him in.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to the fact that I came into machine learning through linguistics. Before I was doing any of this, I was really interested in how language works, how grammar is structured, why languages look the way they do. And when I started working with neural networks, the thing that nagged at me was this: we had these models that could clearly do something with language, often better than the systems we had carefully built by hand, and yet nobody could tell you what they were doing. That felt like an unfinished question rather than a solved one.

So interpretability was the natural place to go, because it's the part of the field that actually asks the "why." Not just "does the model get the answer right," but "what representation did it build, what computation did it run, and can we find that inside the weights or the activations." For someone with a linguistics background, that's very familiar. Linguists spend their whole careers trying to infer hidden structure from surface behavior. You can't see grammar directly, you have to design clever experiments and probes to reveal it. Interpretability is the same instinct pointed at a different object.

The other piece is that I like work where the tools themselves are part of the contribution. A lot of my research has been on methods, things like causal intervention and representation editing, where the goal is to build a reliable way to ask a model a question and get a trustworthy answer back. That appeals to me because it compounds. A good method lets a hundred other people ask questions you never thought of.

And then, more practically, I think it matters. If these systems are going to be deployed everywhere, and they are, then being able to say what's going on inside them isn't a luxury. It's the difference between engineering and alchemy. So it felt like the place where my curiosity, my background, and something actually important all lined up.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he wanted to know what neural networks were doing and describes interpretability as investigating their representations and computations, conveying a desire to understand how AI systems work.

astra-6.text: For me, the appeal is the gap between what a model can do and what we understand about how it does it. You can observe its behavior, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what’s happening internally. Interpretability turns that curiosity into a research question: can we identify the mechanisms behind a behavior and test whether our explanation is actually right? That combination of understanding something and putting the explanation to the test is what makes it a natural direction for me.

r001.rationale: He says he is drawn to interpretability by wanting to understand what is happening inside models and identify the mechanisms behind their behavior.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it’s the combination of wanting to understand how something works and wanting that understanding to be useful. With language models, we can observe what they do, but it’s much harder to explain how they arrived at a particular answer. That gap is really interesting to me. Interpretability offers a way to investigate what’s happening inside the model, with the hope that understanding those mechanisms will help us identify failures and make models more reliable.

r001.rationale: He says he wants to understand how language models work and investigate what is happening inside them, which conveys his desire to understand the principles underlying AI systems.
